title: Ten languages share a fast turn target, and differ in tempo
body: Stivers, Enfield, and colleagues (2009) measured the offset between a polar question and its response in video of informal talk in 10 languages. A positive offset is a gap. A negative offset is overlap. Each language's distribution was unimodal, with its mode between 0 and +200 ms. The overall mode was 0 ms. The overall median was +100 ms. The mean for the whole set was +208 ms. Japanese was the fastest mean (+7 ms) and Danish the slowest (+469 ms). Language means sat within about 250 ms of that cross-language mean. The authors' reading is a shared avoidance of overlap and a shared minimization of silence, with cultural differences that are quantitative. They also report that, in a Dutch corpus, timing after questions and after non-questions did not differ, so they treat the question-answer pair as a proxy for turn-taking more generally. Ethnographic claims of radically different systems (very long Nordic silences, or overlap as the Antiguan norm) are the hypothesis this measurement did not support.

contested_views.position: Some ethnographic reports describe cultures whose ordinary talk is built on long silences, or on simultaneous speech, rather than on a minimal-gap minimal-overlap target.
contested_views.source: The reports Stivers and colleagues cite and then test, including Reisman on Antigua and Lehtonen and Sajavaara on Nordic silence.
